lead: At microwave frequencies a component is not measured with a multimeter. Power enters and leaves through ports, and a port is a transmission-line cross-section with a fixed reference impedance Z₀, usually 50 Ω. The scattering matrix collects the ratios of outgoing to incoming waves. It describes amplifiers, filters, couplers and antennas near 1–30 GHz, where open and short circuits are hard to apply. Engineers read S-parameters from a vector network analyser and use them in design.
prereq: You need: travelling waves, reflection coefficient and VSWR from reflection coefficient, standing waves and VSWR.

sections.h3: Waves in and out of a port

blocks.text: At low frequency we use voltage V and current I. Above about 1 GHz the connecting lines behave as transmission lines, so a wave picture is easier. At port i, define aᵢ as the wave travelling into the component and bᵢ as the wave travelling out. Both are normalised so |aᵢ|² and |bᵢ|² are powers in watts.

blocks.where: Vᵢ and Iᵢ are the total voltage and current at port i; Z₀ is the real reference impedance, usually 50 Ω; aᵢ is the incident wave and bᵢ is the outgoing wave.

blocks.text: For N ports the outgoing waves are linear combinations of the incoming waves: b = S a. The element Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ / aⱼ with every port except j terminated in a matched load, so aₖ = 0 for k ≠ j. This ratio is a complex number: its magnitude gives amplitude and its angle gives phase. The array S is the scattering matrix; some syllabi call it the scattering matrix.

The definition exists because a matched load is easy to build and repeat at microwave frequencies; a perfect open or short is not. S-parameters also connect directly to power, so return loss, gain and isolation follow from |Sᵢⱼ|.

sections.h3: The four S-parameters of a two-port

blocks.text: For a two-port, match port 2 (a₂ = 0) and drive port 1. Then b₁ = S₁₁a₁ and b₂ = S₂₁a₁. So S₁₁ is the input reflection coefficient and S₂₁ is the forward voltage gain. Match port 1 (a₁ = 0) and drive port 2: b₁ = S₁₂a₂ and b₂ = S₂₂a₂. S₂₂ is the output reflection coefficient; S₁₂ is the reverse voltage gain.

items: S₁₁ = input reflection coefficient with port 2 matched.
S₂₁ = forward voltage gain with port 2 matched.
S₁₂ = reverse voltage gain with port 1 matched.
S₂₂ = output reflection coefficient with port 1 matched.

blocks.text: The signal-flow graph shows the same four paths. A wave a₁ can reflect at port 1 through S₁₁ or cross to b₂ through S₂₁. A wave a₂ can cross to b₁ through S₁₂ or reflect at port 2 through S₂₂.

blocks.text: Reciprocity: a passive component with no ferrite or active material has S = Sᵀ, so S₁₂ = S₂₁. Losslessness: a lossless component obeys S†S = I, where S† is the conjugate transpose and I is the identity matrix. This means the total power leaving equals the total power entering. Matched: all diagonal terms Sᵢᵢ = 0.

The reference plane matters. If you move a port outward by a line length l, the phase of every S-parameter touching that port changes by e^{−jβl}, where β = 2π/λ is the phase constant and λ is the guided wavelength. S-parameters also depend on frequency and on the reference impedance Z₀. A 50 Ω S-matrix is not valid for a 75 Ω system without renormalisation. Report the frequency and Z₀ with every S-parameter.
For a matched lossless reciprocal two-port, |S₂₁| = 1 and S₁₁ = S₂₂ = 0; a real filter is close to this only in its passband.

figure.caption: The forward path S₂₁ = 0.9 carries most of the wave; S₁₂ = 0 marks a unilateral device, so reverse isolation is ideal.

spec.aria: Signal-flow graph of a two-port: incident wave a₁ at port 1 gives reflected b₁ through S₁₁ = 0.2 and transmitted b₂ through S₂₁ = 0.9; incident wave a₂ gives reverse b₁ through S₁₂ = 0 and reflected b₂ through S₂₂ = 0.1.

examples.question: A 50 Ω two-port at 10 GHz has S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, S₂₁ = 0.9∠−30°, S₁₂ = 0, S₂₂ = 0.1∠0°. Find (a) return loss at port 1, (b) insertion loss, (c) input VSWR when port 2 is matched, and (d) reverse isolation.
steps: Port 2 is matched, so a₂ = 0. The input reflection coefficient is Γin = S₁₁ = 0.2∠0°, hence |S₁₁| = 0.2.
Forward magnitude |S₂₁| = 0.9. Insertion loss: IL = −20 log₁₀(0.9) = −20 × (−0.04576) = 0.9151 dB ≈ 0.92 dB. The phase −30° does not change loss.
S₁₂ = 0, so reverse isolation = −20 log₁₀(0) → ∞ dB. This is an ideal unilateral device: no signal travels from port 2 to port 1.
examples.answer: Return loss = 13.98 dB, insertion loss = 0.92 dB, input VSWR = 1.5, and reverse isolation = ∞ dB (ideal).
examples.check:
import math
s11 = 0.2
s21 = 0.9
rl = -20 * math.log10(abs(s11))
il = -20 * math.log10(abs(s21))
vswr = (1 + abs(s11)) / (1 - abs(s11))
print(round(rl, 2))
print(round(il, 2))
print(round(vswr, 2))

traps: Using |S₂₁| directly as dB gain. Convert with 20 log₁₀|S₂₁|; a magnitude of 0.9 is not 0.9 dB.
Forgetting that all other ports must be matched when measuring Sᵢⱼ. If port 2 is not matched, b₁/a₁ is not S₁₁; it includes the load reflection.
Ignoring the reference impedance Z₀ and the reference plane. A 50 Ω S-matrix does not apply directly to a 75 Ω system, and added line length shifts phase.
Confusing S₁₂ with S₂₁. S₂₁ is forward transmission; S₁₂ is reverse transmission. A value S₁₂ = 0 means no reverse path, not no forward path.
Treating |S₁₁| as VSWR. |S₁₁| is the reflection coefficient magnitude; VSWR = (1 + |S₁₁|)/(1 − |S₁₁|).

quiz.a: S₂₁ = b₂/a₁ with port 2 matched, so a₂ = 0. It is the forward voltage gain from port 1 to port 2.

quiz.q: Why must every other port be terminated in a matched load when measuring Sᵢⱼ?
quiz.a: The definition Sᵢⱼ = bᵢ/aⱼ requires aₖ = 0 for k ≠ j. A matched load absorbs the outgoing wave at each other port, so no wave returns to mix with the response being measured.

quiz.q: A two-port has |S₁₁| = 0.1 and |S₂₁| = 0.5 at its design frequency. Find the return loss, input VSWR and insertion loss.
A reciprocal two-port has S₁₁ = S₂₂ = 0 and |S₂₁| = 1. Is it lossless? Explain using the losslessness condition.
quiz.a: For a reciprocal two-port S₁₂ = S₂₁. With S₁₁ = S₂₂ = 0 and |S₂₁| = 1, the matrix satisfies S†S = I: the columns are orthonormal. It is an ideal matched lossless two-port.

quiz.q: An attenuator has |S₂₁| = 0.316. Find its insertion loss in dB.
quiz.a: IL = −20 log₁₀(0.316) = 10.0 dB. A magnitude of 0.316 corresponds to 10 dB loss.

quiz.q: A ferrite isolator has S₁₂ = 0 and S₂₁ = 0.9. Is it reciprocal? What does the reverse isolation equal?
quiz.a: No. Reciprocity requires S₁₂ = S₂₁. Here S₁₂ ≠ S₂₁, so the ferrite bias has broken reciprocity. Reverse isolation = −20 log₁₀(0) → ∞ dB in the ideal case.

quiz.q: State the condition for a lossless N-port in terms of its S-matrix.
quiz.a: S†S = I, where S† is the conjugate transpose of S and I is the identity matrix. Equivalently, S is unitary.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, S-parameters are stored as Touchstone files such as .s2p, one block per frequency, and a vector network analyser writes them after calibration. Modern design flows convert S-parameters to time-domain impulse responses or to mixed-mode S-parameters for differential lines. On-chip MMIC design uses N-port S-matrices with many ports, and de-embedding removes fixture effects. Search for 'Touchstone file format', 'mixed-mode S-parameters' and 'vector network analyser calibration'.
